<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The HSNS&nbsp;&#151; Summus,
Ltd. Business Combination</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On February&nbsp;16, 2001, pursuant to the terms of the Asset
Purchase Agreement, HSNS and Summus, Ltd. effected a business
combination whereby HSNS, as the legal acquirer, purchased
substantially all the assets and operations of Summus, Ltd. This
transaction was recorded as a business combination under
APB&nbsp;16.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
From Summus, Ltd.&#146;s perspective, the primary business
purpose of entering into the transaction with HSNS was to
provide a vehicle for raising capital. Summus, Ltd. was at a
stage in its development where it required additional financing
or needed to combine with another entity in order to finance its
business and realize its other objectives. The business
combination with HSNS became the most logical course of action to

</FONT></DIV>

objectives in view of, among other things, the following:

In addition, Summus, Ltd. evaluated potential financing

20,593,352&nbsp;shares (55.5%) of the Company&#146;s common
stock on an as-converted basis, approximately 53.1% on a

common stock received in the transaction to the shareholders of

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In addition to the items described above, the terms of the Asset
Purchase Agreement provided for HSNS&#146;s assumption of
approximately $2.8&nbsp;million of liabilities of Summus, Ltd.
to third parties. All amounts owed by and between HSNS and
Summus, Ltd. were cancelled upon the closing of the combination.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The recorded value of the combination was based on the equity
value of the shares of common stock and other equity securities
HSNS issued to Summus, Ltd. (for distribution to the Summus,
Ltd. shareholders) in the transaction. Since HSNS&#146;s common
stock was traded on the Pink Sheets&#174;, the fair market value
of the shares of such stock (and other equity securities, on an
as-converted basis) issued in the transaction was more readily
determinable than the fair market value of the shares of common
stock of Summus, Ltd., a privately-held company, exchanged in
consideration for such shares of HSNS common stock and other
equity securities.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The value of the shares of the HSNS common stock and the other
equity securities issued in the transaction was based on the
traded value of such stock on the date of the combination, less
a discount reflecting: (1)&nbsp;the limited public float of the
common stock and (2) the thinly traded volume of HSNS&#146;s
common stock. The discount applied was similar in proportion to
the discount HSNS realized in connection with cash sales of its
common stock to third parties.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Another component of the value of the combination was the value
of the outstanding HSNS stock options. All outstanding HSNS
options on February&nbsp;16, 2001 were treated as replacement
options since the combination was accounted for as a reverse
acquisition with Summus, Ltd. as the accounting acquirer. In
accordance with FASB Interpretation No.&nbsp;44,
<I>&#147;Accounting for Certain Transaction Involving Stock
Compensation&#148;</I> (&#147;FIN 44&#148;), the fair values of
the vested and unvested HSNS options of $4.4&nbsp;million and
$2.3&nbsp;million, respectively, were included as components of
the consideration paid in the transaction. The fair values of
these options were determined using the Black-Scholes
option-pricing model.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Since HSNS was the legal acquirer while Summus, Ltd. was the
accounting acquirer, it was necessary to issue new HSNS stock
options to the existing Summus, Ltd. option holders to reflect
the new capitalization resulting from the transaction. The
number of options issued was determined by comparing the total
consideration received by Summus, Ltd. in the transaction to the
outstanding equity of Summus, Ltd. prior to the transaction.
Since Summus, Ltd. was the accounting acquirer, no value was
ascribed to these options.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Purchase accounting was applied to the assets and liabilities of
HSNS based upon their fair market values as of February&nbsp;16,
2001, the date of the combination. The value of the
consideration described above totaled $23.5 million. The fair
value of the HSNS net liabilities on the date of the combination
totaled approximately $4.0&nbsp;million, resulting in goodwill
valued at approximately $27.5&nbsp;million. The goodwill
recorded in connection with the transaction represented the
excess of the purchase price over the fair value of net assets
acquired in accordance with APB 16. The goodwill is not
associated with specific cash flows of the HSNS assets or
operations acquired. Rather, the goodwill is considered to be
enterprise level goodwill associated with the combined value of
the companies resulting from the combination. The financial
forecasts of the Company demonstrate a sufficient amount of cash
flow to fully realize the amount of recorded goodwill.
Additionally, the market capitalization of the Company of
$94.1&nbsp;million on June&nbsp;30, 2001 does not indicate
impairment of the carrying value of the goodwill. Accordingly,
the Company&#146;s management believes that the amount of
goodwill recorded by the Company in connection with the
acquisition of HSNS was determined in accordance with the
guidance of APB 16 and is recoverable.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

Upon the consummation of the HSNS&nbsp;&#151; Summus, Ltd.
business combination on February&nbsp;16, 2001, the Company
determined to revise its business plan to focus primarily on
Summus, Ltd.&#146;s business operations immediately prior to the
transaction. The Company chose to focus primarily on Summus,
Ltd.&#146;s business plan

because management perceived it had the potential to create

following the first to occur of: (1)&nbsp;payment of $400,000 in
royalty payments to HSNS or (2)&nbsp;ninety days prior to the
second anniversary of the agreement, provided that $400,000 in
royalty payments have been received by HSNS.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The Company&#146;s Current
Business Focus</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The core of the Company&#146;s business plan is to focus on the
emerging wireless and mobile market. We are in the process of
developing multimedia technology to address the bandwidth, error
constraints, contention with voice and data traffic, and power
challenges associated with multimedia content transmission over
existing and future wireless networks. Our technology is based
on certain key mathematical theories and tools, using advances
and results from the fields of wavelets, non-linear partial
differential equations and dynamical systems, and graph theory
and topology. We use these tools to create highly efficient
algorithms for different types of information processing with
low computational complexity and low memory usage.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our strategy is to continue to work toward commercial release of
our BlueFuel&#153; product line currently under
development and to enter into business relationships and
alliances with device manufacturers, content providers and
cellular carriers to extend the reach of multimedia applications
to wireless and mobile devices. It is our intent to license our
technology and provide a framework to those with whom we enter
into such relationships and alliances that will increase usage,
sell devices and increase their customer base. A specific area
of focus will be to identify targeted applications to drive
&#147;market pull&#148; for our products. This will entail
working with select content providers to develop applications
that represent a high likelihood of early adoption by end-users.
These applications will be offered to wireless carriers and
mobile virtual network operators on a revenue-sharing basis. We
believe that this represents a significant opportunity for the
Company to develop an on-going service revenue model.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Although we are in the process of building relationships with
wireless and mobile device manufacturers, content providers and
cellular carriers, we have not, as yet, entered into any
revenue-generating contractual agreements with these parties,
and have not, to date, executed any product orders for the
BlueFuel&#153; product line currently under development.
We recognize that a concern for our corporate viability and the
related concerns regarding our lack of financial resources and
ability to meet specific applications demands and provide
product support may hamper our efforts to forge such business
relationships and alliances. Nevertheless, management believes
that the attributes of our technology will provide opportunities
to enhance our product awareness and profile through such
relationships and alliances.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We are currently focusing our product development resources on
adapting or &#147;porting&#148; BlueFuel&#153; to the
Qualcomm BREW wireless platform. This initial porting effort
will provide the foundation for future ports. This effort is
expected to consume a significant amount of the Company&#146;s
technical and business development resources through the
remainder of 2001. In parallel with this effort, we are
dedicating additional resources to define, develop and execute a
beta/field trial for BlueFuel&#153; Video (our video
compression software for multimedia applications) to support our
internal development efforts and begin to develop market
awareness for BlueFuel&#153;. This beta/field trial is
planned for the fourth quarter of 2001.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We anticipate that the first version of the
BlueFuel&#153; Efficiency Engine&#153; (a
multimedia operating system designed to efficiently route, store
and monitor multimedia traffic in a network) will be available
during the fourth quarter of 2001. We are targeting commercial
release of the BlueFuel&#153; Video solution, including
BlueFuel&#153; Player (player software),
BlueFuel&#153; Create (a content creation tool) and
BlueFuel&#153; Server (the server-side engine) in the
first quarter of 2002.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We anticipate that the various components of the
BlueFuel&#153; product line will be licensed separately or
in combination with one another, with pricing dependent on the
number of components licensed. Our present revenue model
contemplates that wireless carriers or service providers
licensing the BlueFuel&#153; product line would be
assessed a base fee plus a royalty for each subscriber that
signs up to use the service (e.g., by downloading
BlueFuel&#153; Player or accessing
BlueFuel&#153; Server). A further charge would be assessed
if the service provider requires additional servers. In some
cases, we may effectively subsidize the rollout of the
BlueFuel&#153; product line through a revenue sharing
arrangement entered into with a handset manufacturer, content
creator and service provider.

<P align="left">
<B>Results of Operations</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The following discussion and analysis of Summus, Ltd.&#146;s
results of operations and financial condition should be read in
conjunction with Summus, Ltd.&#146;s financial statements and
related notes included in Item&nbsp;13 of this registration
statement on Form&nbsp;10.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">
<B>Six Months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 compared to Six Months
ended June&nbsp;30, 2000</B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Revenues. </I>Total revenues decreased $163,167 to $507,179
in the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001, down 24.3% from
$670,346 in the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2000. The
decrease in these revenues was primarily due to a decrease in
providing contract services.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Costs of Revenues. </I>Total costs of revenues decreased
$51,606 to $235,756 in the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001,
down 18.0% from $287,362 in the corresponding period of the
prior year. Costs of contracts and license fees for the six
months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 and 2000 were comprised
primarily of salaries and related costs of providing such
services.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Gross Profit.</I> Total gross profit decreased $111,561, or
29.1%, to $271,423 for the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001,
compared with $382,984 for the six months ended June&nbsp;30,
2000. The decrease was primarily attributable to less license
fee income in the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 compared
to the corresponding period of the prior year. License fee
income generates a higher gross profit percentage compared to
contract revenues.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Selling, General and Administrative Expenses. </I>Selling,
general and administrative expenses consist primarily of
salaries, consulting fees, office operations, administrative and
general management activities, including legal, accounting and
other professional fees. Selling, general and administrative
expenses for the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001, were
$3,607,288, compared to $2,893,056 for six months ended
June&nbsp;30, 2000. The increase in selling, general and
administrative expenses resulted primarily from the reverse
acquisition transaction.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Amortization Expense.</I> Amortization expense for the six
months ended June 30, 2001, was $3,436,072. During the six
months ended June&nbsp;30, 2000, there was no amortization
expense. The amortization expense recorded in the six months
ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 related to the amortization of the
goodwill resulting from the business combination between HSNS
and Summus, Ltd.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Non-Cash Compensation. </I>Non-cash compensation for the six
months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 was $772,262 compared to
$823,999 for the six months ended June 30, 2000. During the six
months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001, stock options were granted to
employees at prices below the fair value of the underlying
common stock resulting in total compensation of $879,688, of
which $664,438 was charged to expense during the six months
ended June&nbsp;30, 2001. The remaining amount, $215,250, has
been classified as deferred compensation and will be charged to
expense as future vesting of the stock options occurs. The
remaining amount of non-cash compensation for the six months
ended June&nbsp;30, 2001 of $107,824, reflects the amortization
for six months of deferred compensation resulting from stock
options granted during the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000, at
prices below the fair value of the underlying common stock. For
the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2000, amortization of
deferred compensation, resulting from the issuance of stock
options at prices below the fair value of the underlying common
stock, was $823,999. The decrease in amortization of deferred
compensation recorded in the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001
as compared to the corresponding period in the prior year from
options granted in year 2000 is a result of the reversal of
deferred compensation from forfeited stock options during 2001,
plus a large number of fully vested options granted during the
six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2000.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Research and Development. </I>Research and development costs
for the six months ended June&nbsp;30, 2001, were $217,386
compared to $773,913 for the six months ended June&nbsp;30,
2000. The decrease in these costs was due primarily to the
reduced staffing level in the first half of 2001 compared with
that during the comparable period of the prior year.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Summus, Ltd. follows the provisions of AICPA Statement of
Position 97-2, &#147;Software Revenue Recognition,&#148; as
amended by AICPA Statement of Position 98-9 &#147;Modification
of SOP No.&nbsp;97-2 Software Revenue Recognition with respect
to Certain Transactions.&#148; Revenues from software license
fees and hardware sales are generally recognized upon delivery
provided that a contract has been executed, the vendor fee is
fixed or determinable, no significant vendor obligations or
uncertainties surrounding customer acceptance remain, and
collection of the resulting receivable is deemed probable.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Cost of Revenues.</I> Cost of revenues primarily represents
costs of providing contract services. The cost of software
license fee revenue is not separately maintained and
historically has not been significant. Costs of revenues for the
year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000 were $398,326 compared to
$281,254 in the prior year.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Gross Profit.</I> Gross profit for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, was $670,332, representing an increase
of $436,370 over the prior year. The increase in revenues and
gross profit was primarily due to the expansion of government
research projects with the Office of Naval Research,
specifically Summus, Ltd.&#146;s side scan sonar project and
expanded sales efforts with respect to wavelet-based technology
licensing of the company&#146;s photo ID and wavelet-based
software development kit product lines.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Selling, General and Administrative Expenses. </I>Selling,
general and administrative expenses consist primarily of
salaries, consulting fees, office operations, administrative and
general management activities, including legal, accounting and
other professional fees. Selling, general and administrative
expenses for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000, were
$6,221,362 compared to $3,797,067 for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 1999. The increase was primarily due to
increased staffing in sales, marketing, business development,
product development and administrative personnel, in connection
with Summus, Ltd.&#146;s efforts to bring to market finished
products, including the photo ID and wavelet image software
development kits, the MaxxSystem suite of products, and customer
contract work.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Non-Cash Compensation.</I> Non-cash compensation for the year
ended December 31, 2000 was $2,127,962 compared to $2,670,050
for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999. During the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, stock options were granted to directors
and employees at prices below the estimated fair value of the
underlying common stock resulting in total compensation of
$3,106,472, of which $2,127,962 was charged to expense in 2000.
The remaining amount, $978,510, has been classified as deferred
compensation and will be charged to expense as future vesting of
the stock options occurs. Non-cash compensation for the year
ended December&nbsp;31, 1999, resulted from the issuance of
53,401 shares of common stock for services performed by
employees.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Research and Development. </I>Research and development costs
for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000 were $1,119,333
compared to $1,356,686 for the year ended December&nbsp;31,
1999. Such costs consist primarily of the salaries of employees
devoted to research and development activities. The decrease
resulted from a reduction of the research and development staff
that occurred in the second half of 2000. Given Summus,
Ltd.&#146;s financial condition, several research and
development personnel decided to pursue other opportunities.
However, management does not believe the attrition had a
significant adverse effect on its research and development
efforts.

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Gain on Sale of Stock of Equity Investee. </I>Gain on the
sale of stock of equity investee for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000 was $3,680,065 compared to $2,314,390 for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999. In 1999, Summus, Ltd.
acquired 11,042,360 shares of common stock of HSNS. Summus, Ltd.
acquired 1,500,000 shares of HSNS common stock in connection
with HSNS&#146;s issuance of such shares in lieu of a cash
payment of $750,000 due from HSNS under the terms of the
February&nbsp;1999 Marketing License Agreement. Summus, Ltd.
acquired an additional 9,542,360 shares of HSNS common stock
from Mr.&nbsp;Richdale and his affiliates in exchange for
132,888 shares of Summus, Ltd. common stock. The initial
carrying amount of the HSNS shares was recorded at the estimated
fair value of the shares, factoring in a discount associated
with the shares constituting &#147;restricted securities&#148;
that were not freely tradable. During the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, Summus, Ltd. sold 1,171,579 shares of
HSNS common stock for gross proceeds of $4,492,799 (representing
an average price per share of $3.83), resulting in a gain on
sale of $3,680,065. During the year ended December&nbsp;31,
1999, Summus, Ltd. sold 1,653,000 shares of its HSNS common
stock for gross proceeds of $2,977,500 (representing an average
price per share of $1.80), resulting in a gain on sale of
$2,314,390.

<P align="left">
<B>Liquidity and Capital Resources</B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
As of June&nbsp;30, 2001, the Company had $143,567 of cash on
hand and negative working capital of approximately
$5.1&nbsp;million. As of such date, the Company had
approximately $5.2&nbsp;million of accounts payable, accrued
expenses, notes payable and capital lease obligations and was in
default in the aggregate amount of $1.1&nbsp;million with
several of its vendors. The vendors for which more significant
amounts are owed have been contacted. The Company was in
discussions with such vendors for purposes of seeking to
negotiate down the amounts due, extend the payment terms and/or
satisfy amounts due through a combination of cash and stock.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The Company entered into a settlement agreement and release,
dated August&nbsp;7, 2001, with one of such vendors, Analysts
International Corporation (&#147;AIC&#148;), which provided the
Company with computer programming services during the 1999-2000
period. Under the terms of the settlement agreement, the Company
has agreed to pay the sum of $358,426, plus interest accruing at
the rate of 8% per annum from March&nbsp;31, 2000 (the
&#147;Indebtedness&#148;) according to the following payment
schedule: (i)&nbsp;$20,000 upon execution of the settlement
agreement, (ii)&nbsp;$5,000 per month for a period of six
months, commencing one month after execution of the agreement,
and (iii)&nbsp;$10,000 per month until the balance of the
Indebtedness is paid in full.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<P align="left">
<B>New Accounting Pronouncements</B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In June&nbsp;1998, the FASB issued Statement of Financial
Accounting Standards (&#147;SFAS&#148;) No.&nbsp;133,
&#147;Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging
Activities.&#148; SFAS 133 requires that derivative instruments
be recognized as either assets or liabilities in the
consolidated balance sheet based on their fair values. Changes
in the fair values of such derivative instruments will be
recorded either in results of operations or in other
comprehensive income, depending on the intended use of the
derivative instrument. The initial application of SFAS 133 will
be reported as the effect of a change in accounting principle.
SFAS 133 is effective for all fiscal years beginning after
June&nbsp;15, 2000. Because the Company has not historically
used derivative financial instruments, the Company does not
anticipate that SFAS 133 will have a material impact on its
consolidated financial statements.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On June&nbsp;29, 2001, the Financial Accounting Standards Board
(&#147;FASB&#148;) unanimously approved the issuance of
Statements of Financial Accounting Standards (&#147;SFAS&#148;)
No.&nbsp;141, <I>&#147;Business Combinations&#148;</I> and
No.&nbsp;142, <I>&#147;Goodwill and Other Intangible
Assets.&#148;</I> SFAS 141 eliminates the pooling-of-interests
method of accounting for business combinations except for
qualifying business combinations that were initiated prior to
July&nbsp;1, 2001. SFAS 141 also includes new criteria to
recognize intangible assets separately from goodwill. The
requirements of SFAS 141 are effective for any business
combination accounted for by the purchase method that is
completed after June&nbsp;30, 2001. Under SFAS 142, goodwill and
intangible assets with indefinite lives are no longer amortized
but are reviewed annually, or more frequently if impairment
indicators arise, for impairment. Separable intangible assets
that are not deemed to have an indefinite life will continue to
be amortized over their useful lives. The amortization
provisions of SFAS 142 requiring non-amortization of goodwill
and indefinite-lived intangible assets apply to goodwill and
indefinite-lived intangible assets acquired after June&nbsp;30,
2001. With respect to goodwill and intangible assets acquired
prior to July&nbsp;1, 2001, the Company will adopt SFAS 142 in
the fiscal year beginning January&nbsp;1, 2002, and therefore
cease all amortization of goodwill as of January 1, 2002. The
effect of adopting SFAS 142 by the Company beginning
January&nbsp;1, 2002 will result in not recording amortization
of approximately $9.2&nbsp;million in 2002 of the goodwill
resulting from the business combination between HSNS and Summus,
Ltd. on February&nbsp;16, 2001 that otherwise would have been
recorded.

<B>High Speed Net Solutions, Inc.</B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The following discussion is qualified in its entirety by, and

the notes thereto appearing elsewhere in this registration

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
As discussed in Note 2 to HSNS&#146;s consolidated financial
statements, HSNS has restated its consolidated financial
statements for the fiscal year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999. The
following discussion gives effect to the restatement.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">
<B>Overview</B>

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Acquisition of Marketers
World, Inc./ Brad Richdale Direct, Inc.</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
HSNS was originally incorporated in 1984 under the name of EMN
Enterprises, Inc. EMN Enterprises remained a non-operating shell
company until August&nbsp;1998. In August&nbsp;1998, EMN
Enterprises acquired all the assets (with a book value of
$495,259) and assumed the liabilities (in the amount of $75,000)
of Marketers World, Inc., a private company that intended to
engage in leasing computer systems to businesses and performing
related services. Upon acquiring the Marketers World assets,
HSNS changed its name to Zzap.net.inc. Marketers World received
10,000,000 shares of EMN Enterprises&#146; common stock in the
transaction, of which EMN Enterprises issued 9,275,000 shares
and Mr.&nbsp;Rene Hamouth, the then President of EMN
Enterprises, transferred 725,000 shares. Upon distribution of
the shares received in the transaction by Marketers World,
Ormond Trust, an affiliate of Mr.&nbsp;Richdale, held a
controlling interest in EMN Enterprises. At the time of the
transaction, EMN Enterprises had no assets or liabilities and,
accordingly, the transaction was accounted for as a
recapitalization of HSNS. Since the acquisition was accounted
for as a recapitalization of EMN Enterprises, the shares of its
common stock issued in the transaction were not valued and,
consequently, no goodwill was recorded.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In September&nbsp;1998, Zzap.net.inc. issued a total of
1,000,000 shares of its common stock in partial consideration
for all the issued and outstanding shares of capital stock of
Brad Richdale Direct, Inc. (&#147;BRD&#148;). Of the shares
issued in the transaction, 775,000 shares were issued to Ormond
Trust, valued at $77,500, and 225,000 shares were issued to
Michael Cimino, the then President of both BRD and
Zzap.net.inc., in consideration for services rendered. The
primary purpose of this transaction was to obtain licensing and
marketing rights, held by BRD, to certain products under
development by Summus, Ltd. Zzap.net.inc. intended to use these
products in connection with the planned operations of Marketers
World. Since BRD had nominal assets and operations, this
transaction was accounted for as an acquisition of licensing
rights, rather than as a business combination. The value
attributed to this transaction was based on recent transactions
in Zzap.net.inc.&#146;s common stock near the date of the
transaction.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
By year-end 1998, Zzap.net.inc., in part because of its limited
financial resources, determined to discontinue the operations of
the former Marketers World business. Accordingly, the net book
value of the assets associated with this business, in the amount
of $68,890, was written off at December&nbsp;31, 1998 as part of
the loss from discontinued operations. Coincident with that
decision, Zzap.net.inc. changed its name to High Speed Net
Solutions, Inc.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The Marketing License
Agreement with Summus, Ltd.</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In February&nbsp;1999, HSNS entered into the Marketing License
Agreement (&#147;MLA&#148;) with Summus, Ltd. under which HSNS
obtained rights to resell stand-alone software products
specified in the MLA over the three-year term of the agreement.
In consideration for such rights, HSNS agreed to pay an upfront
royalty payment of $3,000,000, to be paid in four installments
of $750,000 each, the first such payment due upon execution of
the MLA and the last three payments due in monthly intervals at
the end of each of the three months thereafter.
Mr.&nbsp;Richdale paid all but $60,000 of the first three
payments under the agreement on HSNS&#146;s behalf. HSNS issued
convertible debentures in the aggregate principal amount of
$2,157,998 to Mr.&nbsp;Richdale or entities he controlled in
partial consideration for such payments. HSNS issued
1.5&nbsp;million shares of its common stock to Summus, Ltd. in
lieu of the final cash payment due under the MLA.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="center">47

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Since each of the four products specified under the MLA was
completed and ready for resale, HSNS capitalized the upfront
royalty payment, in the amount of $4,528,125 (representing the
cash payments of $2,250,000 and 1.5&nbsp;million shares of
HSNS&#146;s common stock valued at $2,278,125), as prepaid
software royalties (essentially license fees) in accordance with
the provisions of Statement of Financial Standards No.&nbsp;86,
&#147;Accounting for the Costs of Computer Software to Be Sold,
Leased, or Otherwise Marketed,&#148; as each of the four
software products specifically referred to in the MLA had
reached &#147;technological feasibility&#148; within the meaning
of Paragraphs 4 and 38 of that statement. HSNS has since
determined to restate the value of 1.5&nbsp;million shares by
applying a discount to the traded value of HSNS&#146;s common
stock at the time of issuance based on the discount associated
with private sales of shares of its common stock (such shares
being &#147;restricted securities&#148; as defined in
Rule&nbsp;144 under the Securities Act of 1933) within close
proximity of the time of the issuance of such shares. The
revaluation of these shares has resulted in a reduction of
$1,528,125 in the original recorded value of the prepaid
royalties (i.e., from $4,528,125 to $3,000,000).

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In August&nbsp;1999, Summus, Ltd. acquired a majority of the
then outstanding shares of common stock of HSNS. Summus, Ltd.
subsequently sold a portion of its shares of HSNS&#146;s common
stock to third parties such that by December&nbsp;31, 1999,
Summus, Ltd.&#146;s interest had been reduced to approximately
44%. In connection with the transaction, Summus, Ltd. replaced
HSNS&#146;s management team with its designees. Over the next
several months, the new management team determined to revise
HSNS&#146;s business plan. Rather than function as a reseller of
Summus, Ltd. software products, management determined that HSNS
should function as an application service provider or service
bureau, utilizing Summus Ltd.&#146;s compression technology to
enhance the effectiveness of e-commerce, digital advertising,
direct marketing campaigns and multimedia&nbsp;&#151; what HSNS
termed &#147;rich media direct&#148; (&#147;RMD&#148;).

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Planned Service Bureau
Business Using Summus, Ltd.&#146;s MaxxSystem</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
As a result of this change in business plan, HSNS entered into
negotiations with Summus, Ltd., beginning in December&nbsp;1999,
to modify the companies&#146; contractual relationship under the
MLA. These negotiations resulted in the companies&#146;
execution of several agreements (i.e., a master agreement,
software license agreement, software maintenance agreement,
revenue sharing agreement and software escrow agreement) in
mid-February&nbsp;2000. These agreements superseded the MLA in
its entirety. Under these agreements, Summus, Ltd. granted to
HSNS a non-exclusive license to use a suite of software products
referred to as &#147;MaxxSystem.&#148;

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Under the new agreements, HSNS did not become obligated to make
any additional payments, in cash or other consideration, to
Summus, Ltd. for the software products to be provided
thereunder. In fact, HSNS received approximately
$2.2&nbsp;million in credits toward future fees due and payable
to Summus, Ltd. Under the circumstances, HSNS determined that,
in the absence of any information that would have indicated that
the net realizable value of any of the products licensed under
the MLA had been adversely affected by its change in business
plan or that the unamortized capitalized costs exceeded the net
realizable value of such products, no impairment-related write
off under SFAS No.&nbsp;86 was appropriate as of
December&nbsp;31, 1999. As of that date, HSNS fully expected to
generate future revenues, in its contemplated service bureau
business, through the use of the Summus, Ltd. software products
covered by the several agreements then being negotiated,
sufficient to recover the carrying value of the prepayments
under the MLA.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The software license agreement provided HSNS with rights to use
of Summus, Ltd.&#146;s MaxxSystem suite of products in
HSNS&#146;s planned service bureau business. The agreement did
not permit HSNS to resell any of the software products
constituting MaxxSystem. As such, HSNS determined that the
MaxxSystem suite of software products constituted &#147;internal
use&#148; software subject to Statement of Position
(&#147;SOP&#148;) 98-1, &#147;Accounting for the Costs of
Computer Software Developed or Obtained for Internal Use.&#148;
Although the software license agreement (and the related
agreements) were executed in mid-February&nbsp;2000, the terms
of such agreement had been substantially negotiated and agreed
to at the time HSNS&#146;s financial statements as of and for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999, were issued in
February&nbsp;2000. For this reason, HSNS also gave
consideration to the question of impairment of the prepaid
royalties as of December&nbsp;31, 1999, under the provisions of
SOP&nbsp;98-1. SOP&nbsp;98-1 requires an evaluation of
capitalized software costs for impairment in accordance with
SFAS&nbsp;121. SFAS&nbsp;121 requires an estimate of future cash
flows to determine if an asset that is

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="center">48

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left">
in use is impaired. SOP 98-1 includes examples of indicators
that internal use software has been impaired, including:
(i)&nbsp;the software is not expected to provide substantive
service potential; (ii)&nbsp;a change occurs in the extent or
manner in which the software is used or expected to be used; or
(iii)&nbsp;a significant change to the software is made or
expected to be made. The change in HSNS&#146;s business plan was
driven primarily by the view that delivery of multimedia over
the Internet through use of the MaxxSystem suite of software
products offered greater future cash flows than the resale of
the software products licensed under the MLA. As noted above,
under the agreements HSNS did not become obligated to make any
additional payments, in cash or other consideration, to Summus,
Ltd. for the software products to be provided thereunder. In
fact, HSNS received approximately $2.2&nbsp;million in credits
from the prepaid royalties paid in connection with the MLA
toward future fees due and payable to Summus under the terms of
the master agreement. In view of these considerations, HSNS
determined that an impairment-related write-off of the prepaid
royalties was not appropriate as of December&nbsp;31, 1999 under
SOP 98-1 and SFAS 121.
</DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
HSNS has concluded it is appropriate to restate the accompanying
financial statements as of and for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 1999, to reduce the recorded value of the
prepaid royalties by $833,333 to reflect the amortization of the
prepaid software royalties in 1999 in accordance with the
provisions of SFAS No.&nbsp;86. Originally, no amortization was
recorded as HSNS planned to directly offset the prepaid
royalties against future royalty payments otherwise due under
the terms of the MLA. The amount amortized was derived based
upon the downward adjustment in the prepaid royalties carrying
amount associated with the revaluation of the shares of
HSNS&#146;s common stock and applying the straight-line method
over the three-year estimated economic life of the products
licensed under the MLA.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
As explained in Item&nbsp;1. &#147;Business&nbsp;&#151; Our
History,&#148; toward the end of the first quarter of 2000, a
combination of market conditions and potential government
regulatory actions caused HSNS to modify its short- and
longer-term plans for revenue generation as an application
service provider of multimedia content over the Internet. Market
resistance developed to the delivery of Internet services via
&#147;.exe&#148; file types following certain software
vendors&#146; delivery of such files with viruses. This prompted
many companies to configure firewalls to block all files with an
 .exe extension. This limited the market for e-mail distribution
using the MaxxNote (i.e., the video e-mail) module of
MaxxSystem. At about the same time, the Federal Trade Commission
initiated an investigation into the use of information gathered
by permission-based marketing through e-mails and banner ads. In
addition, feedback from HSNS&#146;s early distribution and
campaign management service offerings made evident that HSNS
needed to add to its service offerings video streaming (together
with the computer hardware, network and support facilities to
enable use of video streaming) to be a viable player in the
marketplace.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
In view of these developments, on March&nbsp;28, 2000, HSNS
engaged Nexgenix, an e-business systems integrator, to evaluate
HSNS&#146;s business model and one specific planned application
of MaxxSystem: distribution and campaign management services. In
May&nbsp;2000, Nexgenix presented to HSNS the results of its
evaluation and recommended three software solutions for
distribution and campaign software for HSNS&#146;s service
bureau business. The recommended solutions did not include
MaxxServer, the MaxxSystem module designed to facilitate
distribution and campaign management applications. Based on the
Nexgenix presentation, HSNS&#146;s management determined to
select another vendor&#146;s product to provide the distribution
and campaign management functionality for HSNS&#146;s service
bureau business. Nexgenix&#146;s evaluation did not affect the
other modules of MaxxSystem. Indeed, the MaxxSystem suite of
software products, utilizing Summus, Ltd.&#146;s wavelet-based
technology, continued to represent the primary tool that HSNS
anticipated would drive its service bureau business. For this
reason, at the time of filing its Form&nbsp;10-Q for the
quarterly period ended March&nbsp;31, 2000, HSNS&#146;s
management did not believe any impairment of the carrying value
of its capitalized software license fees relating to the
MaxxSystem software had occurred.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Based on Nexgenix&#146;s recommendations, in July&nbsp;2000 HSNS
licensed software developed by E.Piphany for the distribution
and campaign management functions of its service delivery. The
E.Piphany product was selected as a more robust management and
delivery vehicle for HSNS&#146;s &#147;rich media direct&#148;
(RMD)&nbsp;2.0 and future releases of RMD service offerings. One
of the key criteria for selecting the E.Piphany software was
that HSNS would continue to be able to use the MaxxNote module
as part of RMD 1.0 and future releases of RMD service offerings.
This was consistent with HSNS&#146;s strategy to maximize the
use of Summus, Ltd.&#146;s.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="center">49

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left">
wavelet-based technology in its service offerings, since HSNS
believed that wavelet-based technology would provide it with a
competitive advantage over other service providers in its
contemplated target market.
</DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On June&nbsp;27, 2000, HSNS ran its first e-mail campaign, for
Buy It Now.com, using the MaxxNote component of MaxxSystem. This
was a test campaign, for which HSNS received no fees. In
July&nbsp;2000, HSNS generated revenues of $4,000 by running a
RMD 1.0 campaign for Continental Airlines. Thus, at the end of
the second quarter of 2000, HSNS was proceeding toward
implementation of its service bureau business and management
concluded that no impairment charge was warranted as of
June&nbsp;30, 2000.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The customer analysis and feedback from both the Buy It Now.com
and Continental Airlines campaigns made evident that video
streaming (together with the computer hardware, network and
support facilities to enable use of video streaming) needed to
be added to HSNS&#146;s service delivery in order to make its
service business more viable in the marketplace. Summus, Ltd.
was obligated to provide the streaming software (i.e.,
MaxxServer) under the terms of the software license agreement.
However, since the MaxxServer component of MaxxSystem was not
yet completed and HSNS did not have the required infrastructure
in place, HSNS commenced a search for a total streaming and
related infrastructure solution. Although MaxxServer was not yet
finalized at the time, Summus, Ltd. was in the process of
completing this module of MaxxSystem. In January&nbsp;2001
Summus, Ltd. delivered a beta version of its streaming software
to HSNS for use in its service delivery demonstration.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Following a search for a total streaming and infrastructure
solution, HSNS, in September&nbsp;2000, entered into a licensing
agreement with All Video Network, Inc. (&#147;AVN&#148;) to
secure both the streaming and the required infrastructure to
conduct streaming. AVN provided a full streaming service.
HSNS&#146;s management anticipated that Summus, Ltd.&#146;s
wavelet-based technology would be integrated into this full
streaming service when Summus, Ltd. completed its software
development. AVN&#146;s real value to HSNS was in the
infrastructure AVN provided to HSNS, enabling it to gain a
quicker entry into this market. AVN&#146;s streaming service was
considered a complementary, not a substitute, solution, because
although it had the capability to stream wavelet-based
compressed media (as well as MPEG4, an industry-leading
compression technology), it did not have the capability to
capture statistics, develop content or compress content using
wavelets. This functionality was core to MaxxSystem.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

possible indicator of impairment of the capitalized software

statements. However, this potential impairment indicator was
overcome by the following:

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The HSNS&nbsp;&#151; Summus,
Ltd. Business Combination</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Because HSNS viewed Summus, Ltd.&#146;s compression technology
as key to differentiating HSNS&#146;s rich media direct service
delivery from other service offerings, HSNS entered into
discussions with Summus, Ltd. that led to the two companies
entering into the Asset Purchase Agreement at the end of October
2000. The transaction was contingent on HSNS raising
$7.5&nbsp;million within 60 days. HSNS was not able to raise the
necessary funding to close the transaction within the required
time frame. Due to the lack of funding, HSNS had to temporarily
delay its implementation and testing of MaxxSystem in 2000 and
became unable to effect payments to third party vendors who were
critical in completing this process.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Since HSNS could not raise the stipulated amount of additional
capital, management determined that it was unlikely that funding
would be available to develop and rollout the service bureau
business model as previously planned. Under FASB 121, when it is
no longer probable that computer software will be placed in
service, the software should be reported at the lower of its
carrying amount or fair value. Under SOP 98-1, there is a
rebuttable presumption that if there are no plans to complete
the software or place it in service, the software has a fair
value of zero. SOP 98-1 describes several indicators that the
software may no longer be expected to be completed and placed in
service, including &#147;a lack of expenditures budgeted or
incurred for the project.&#148; Therefore, during the fourth
quarter of 2000, management determined that the assets
associated with HSNS&#146;s service bureau business (other than
the assets of Douglas May&nbsp;&#38;&nbsp;Co.) were impaired.
Accordingly, an impairment charge of approximately
$2.9&nbsp;million was recorded in the fourth quarter of 2000
consisting of the net carrying value of the capitalized costs
associated with MaxxSystem of approximately $2.2&nbsp;million
and other capitalized costs incurred in the development of the
service bureau business of approximately $0.7&nbsp;million.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On February&nbsp;16, 2001, HSNS and Summus, Ltd. consummated the
transactions contemplated by the Asset Purchase Agreement,
without HSNS having secured any additional capital. The
agreements entered into in mid-February&nbsp;2000 by the
companies were cancelled in their entirety. Following the
combination, the Company revised its business plan, consistent
with the Summus, Ltd. business plan at the time of the
transaction, to focus on applications of the acquired
compression software and technology in the mobile and wireless
Internet market.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Acquisition of Douglas May
&#38; Co., Inc.</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
On July&nbsp;10, 2000, under the terms of a share acquisition
agreement dated as of June&nbsp;30, 2000, by and between HSNS
and Douglas May, HSNS acquired all of the issued and outstanding
capital stock of Douglas May &#38; Co. by issuing to Mr. May
183,070 shares of HSNS common stock in a business combination
accounted for as a purchase.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The acquisition of Douglas May &#38; Co. was made in order to
supplement HSNS&#146;s planned rich media direct business. This
acquisition was expected to create synergies with HSNS&#146;s
planned rich media direct service offering.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The shares of HSNS common stock issued in the transaction were
valued at $1,376,000. Under the terms of the share acquisition
agreement, the 183,070 shares of HSNS common stock were issued
in three allotments. The first allotment corresponded to
$500,000 of value. At closing, HSNS issued 50,000 shares of
common stock, the number of such shares being subject to
adjustment if the Over-the-Counter Bulletin Board&#174; trading
price of the common stock on the first anniversary of the
closing date of the transaction was less than $10.00 per share.
Under such circumstances, HSNS was obligated to issue additional
shares of common stock that, when added to the 50,000 shares,
and multiplied by the per share trading price on the first
anniversary of the closing date, equaled $500,000 in value. The
issuance of the 50,000 shares was recorded at the
&#147;guaranteed&#148; amount of $10.00 per share on the date of
issuance, July&nbsp;10, 2000. Payment or issuance of any
additional shares under the terms of the share acquisition
agreement will not change the recorded cost of the acquisition
of Douglas May &#38; Co.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The second allotment of shares of common stock (87,498 shares)
issued at closing corresponded to $576,000 of value. HSNS
committed to file a registration statement with the SEC to
register the resale of these shares. If the shares were not
freely tradable on or before January&nbsp;1, 2001, Mr.&nbsp;May
had the right to cause HSNS to repurchase these shares from him
by making six cash installment payments totaling $576,000. As of
December&nbsp;31, 2000, Mr.&nbsp;May had not yet elected to have
HSNS repurchase these shares.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The third allotment of shares of common stock (45,572 shares)
issued at closing corresponded to $300,000 of value. HSNS
committed to file a registration statement with the SEC to
register the resale of these shares. If the shares were not
freely tradable on or before the expiration of 90&nbsp;days from
the closing date, Mr.&nbsp;May had the right to cause HSNS to
repurchase these shares from him by releasing funds, in the
amount of $300,000, which the share acquisition agreement
provided be placed into an escrow account, the funds being from
certain accounts receivable of Douglas May&nbsp;&#38; Co. that
were collected subsequent to the acquisition date. In
January&nbsp;2001, based on the election of Mr.&nbsp;May, HSNS
repurchased and retired these shares for $300,000 using the
funds from the escrow account. These shares were treated as
outstanding for loss per share purposes in accordance with the
guidance set forth in SFAS No.&nbsp;128. All shares issued that
are subject to repurchase by HSNS have been presented on
HSNS&#146;s balance sheet as redeemable stock outside of
shareholder&#146;s equity.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The results of operations of Douglas May &#38; Co. are included
in HSNS&#146;s operations from the date of acquisition. HSNS
recorded goodwill in the amount of $1,174,437 related to this
acquisition.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During 2000 Douglas May &#38; Co. produced negative cash flows.
Because of HSNS&#146;s decision in the fourth quarter of 2000
not to further pursue the planned rich media direct business due
to funding constraints, management determined there was no basis
upon which to project positive future cash flows from Douglas
May &#38; Co. since the basis for making the acquisition was
originally related to expected synergies and expected future
prospects by incorporating the business of Douglas May &#38; Co.
into the planned rich media direct business. Thus, in accordance
with the provisions of SFAS 121, HSNS concluded that the
unamortized portion of the goodwill recorded in connection with
the acquisition of Douglas May &#38; Co. ($1,058,177, net of the
previously amortized amount of $116,260) had become fully
impaired and should be written off. HSNS recorded an impairment
charge of $1,058,177 in the fourth quarter of 2000 to recognize
the unamortized balance of goodwill written-off.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

<P align="left">

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Revenues. </I>Revenues for the year ended December&nbsp;31,
2000, of $599,054 represent revenues by Douglas May &#38; Co.
and the $4,000 generated from the rich media direct campaign run
for Continental Airlines. Revenue from the media creation
services provided by Douglas May &#38; Co., including creative

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Costs of Revenues.</I> Costs of revenues for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, associated with Douglas May &#38; Co.,
were $476,280.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<I>Gross Profit.</I> Gross profit for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, was $122,774.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
During most of the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999, HSNS was
positioning itself to engage in the resale of the various
software products licensed from Summus, Ltd. under the
February&nbsp;1999 Marketing License Agreement. HSNS engaged in
the development of a sales and marketing plan for these products
and endeavored to put in place the necessary infrastructure.
However, 1999 was characterized by several management changes,
including the change that followed Summus, Ltd.&#146;s acquiring
a controlling interest in HSNS in August. Further, HSNS&#146;s
limited financial resources greatly hampered its marketing and
sales efforts. Of necessity, HSNS made such efforts primarily
from its website. In view of these disruptions and constraints,
HSNS did not realize any revenues from these products. As
described in Item&nbsp;1.
&#147;Business&nbsp;&#151;&nbsp;Overview,&#148; by year-end HSNS
had determined to change its business plan and was in the midst
of negotiations with Summus, Ltd. to modify its existing
business relationship.

ended December&nbsp;31, 2000, included $1,754,560 in legal and

Related Stockholder Matters&nbsp;&#151; OTC Bulletin Board

the remaining portion was attributable to professional fees
associated with Securities and Exchange Commission filings and
other general corporate activity. Selling, general and
administrative expenses for the year ended December&nbsp;31,
2000, also included $1,498,792 in salaries and payroll costs and
$860,602 in outside consulting fees. The remaining balance is
attributable to the development and rollout of HSNS&#146;s
planned service bureau business.

<I>Loss Contingency Charges. </I>Loss contingency charges for
the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2000 were $1,281,946 compared
to $800,000 for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999. On
January&nbsp;26, 2000, William R. Dunavant
(&#147;Dunavant&#148;), a former shareholder of Summus
Technologies, Inc., who received 350,000 shares of HSNS&#146;s
common stock and $100,000 in cash in exchange for his shares of
Summus Technologies, Inc. stock, filed a lawsuit against HSNS.
Former management of HSNS had entered into an agreement with
Dunavant and Michael Cimino, the former President of HSNS, that
obligated HSNS to file a registration statement with the SEC to
register the resale of these shares within a specified time
period. HSNS&#146;s failure to register such shares resulted in
a lawsuit against HSNS seeking damages of $13,300,000. Pursuant
to a settlement agreement entered into as of May&nbsp;4, 2000,
as amended on June&nbsp;6, 2000, HSNS agreed, among other
things, to register the 350,000 shares then held by Dunavant and
to issue to him an aggregate of 175,000 new shares of
HSNS&#146;s common stock with registration rights. HSNS
subsequently entered into a Second Amended and Restated
Settlement Agreement, dated October 26, 2000, which superseded
all previous agreements with Dunavant. By the terms of the
Second Amended and Restated Settlement Agreement (and a
supplemental letter thereto, dated December&nbsp;5, 2000), HSNS
issued to Dunavant 1,700,000 shares of common stock in 2000. The
value of these shares, totaling $1.6 million, was based on a
discount applied to the traded value of HSNS&#146;s common stock
on the date of issuance reflecting that the shares were not
registered and are, therefore, &#147;restricted securities&#148;
within the meaning of Rule&nbsp;144 under the Securities Act of
1933. The number of common shares held by Dunavant on
December&nbsp;31, 2000, totaled 2,050,000. Additionally, HSNS
became obligated to issue 25,000 shares of restricted common
stock per month and pay $25,000 in cash per month to Dunavant
until a registration statement on Form&nbsp;S-1, covering the
resale of Dunavant&#146;s shares, is declared effective by the
SEC. Accordingly, the loss contingency for the year ended
December&nbsp;31, 2000, included the value of the shares issued
to Dunavant in 2000, plus management&#146;s best estimate of the
monthly share and cash allotments HSNS is obligated to make
until a registration statement on Form&nbsp;S-1 is declared
effective by the SEC. See the disclosure under Item&nbsp;7.
&#147;Certain Relationships and Related Transactions.&#148;

the fourth quarter of 2000 consisting of the net carrying amount
of the capitalized costs incurred in the development of the
service bureau business. Included in these costs was
approximately $2.2&nbsp;million of costs associated with
MaxxSystem and $0.7&nbsp;million of other capitalized costs
incurred in the development of the service bureau business. See

<P align="left">
<B>Item 3.&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Properties.</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our principal executive offices are located at 434 Fayetteville
Street Mall, Suite&nbsp;600, Raleigh, North Carolina 27601. We
occupy an aggregate of 19,100 square feet of leased space at
such location under two leases. A lease for 17,189 square feet,
representing the principal executive offices of Summus, Ltd.
prior to the HSNS&#151;Summus, Ltd. business combination,
expires on October&nbsp;31, 2005. The current annual base rent
for such space is approximately $267,000 and will increase to
approximately $313,000 by the last year of the term. We are
obligated to pay additional rent in the amount of roughly $5,900
per month for the seven month period beginning May&nbsp;1, 2001.
The additional rent is for a buildout of this office space in
March 2000. We also lease 1,911 square feet of space in the same
office building, representing the space occupied by HSNS prior
to the combination. The lease term expires on October&nbsp;31,
2005. The current annual base rent for this space is
approximately $33,400. We are obligated to pay additional rent
in the amount of roughly $2,000 per month for the 24-month
period beginning August&nbsp;1, 2001. The additional rent is to
be paid in connection with our termination of the lease of
approximately 4,900 square feet of office space at this location.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
We believe the terms of these leases are consistent with terms
in the local market generally and that the space will be
adequate for our reasonably foreseeable future needs.

6,000 shares of Series&nbsp;B preferred stock issued and
outstanding (of which 2,000 shares are held in escrow under the
terms of the Asset Purchase Agreement. As of that date, we also

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
By the terms of the agreement under which HSNS and Summus, Ltd.
effected the business combination, the size of the
Company&#146;s Board of Directors was to be increased to ten
members immediately following the closing of the transaction.
Post-closing, the Board was to consist of four members from each
of HSNS and Summus, Ltd. Upon the selection of a ninth director
by the 4&nbsp;representatives of HSNS, Ms.&nbsp;Wendi Tush was
to be appointed to the Board as the tenth member. However,
Ms.&nbsp;C. Cristine Wittress (a HSNS member), Mr.&nbsp;Kenneth
Marks (a Summus, Ltd. member), Stuart Diamond (a Summus, Ltd.
member) and Ms.&nbsp;Wendi Tush (a Summus, Ltd. member) have
since resigned as directors of the Company&#146;s Board and the
Board now consists of four directors.

<P align="left">
<B>Business Experience of Directors, Officers and Other Key
Employees</B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>Dr.&nbsp;Bjorn Jawerth </B>has been on our Board of Directors
since February&nbsp;2000 and has served as Co-Chief Executive
Officer, Chief Scientist and President since February&nbsp;2001.
Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth founded Summus, Ltd. in 1991 and was its
Chairman and President until its acquisition by the Company.
Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth received a Masters of Science in mathematics
and statistics, as well as an M.Sc. in technical physics and
electrical engineering in 1974 from Lund Institute of
Technology, Lund, Sweden. He also received his Ph.D. in
mathematics from Lund Institute in 1977. Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth is the
David W. Robinson Palmetto Professor, Professor of Mathematics
and Adjunct Professor of computer science at the University of
South Carolina. He directs a group of approximately 50
researchers in mathematics, computer science, mechanical
engineering and chemistry at the University of South Carolina
and Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.
Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth has more than 30 years of experience as a
consultant in the areas of image processing and finite element
analysis. He has more than 90 publications to his credit in
books and journals.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>Andrew L. Fox </B>was our Chief Executive Officer from
August&nbsp;2000 through February&nbsp;2001 and our acting
President and Chief Executive Officer from August 1999 through
August&nbsp;2000. Mr.&nbsp;Fox has also been a director since
January&nbsp;2000. Mr.&nbsp;Fox was Executive Vice President of
Sales and Marketing for Summus, Ltd. from August&nbsp;1999
through January&nbsp;2000. Although Mr.&nbsp;Fox ceased to be an
executive officer of the Company following the acquisition of
Summus, Ltd.&#146;s assets in February&nbsp;2001, he remains an
employee of the Company, working primarily in the area of sales
and marketing. From December&nbsp;1996 through June 1999,
Mr.&nbsp;Fox was Senior Marketing Manager of RealNetworks, a
provider of software products and services for Internet media
delivery and a pioneer of streaming media systems enabling the
creation, real-time delivery and playback of audio, video and
multimedia content on the Web. From June&nbsp;1991 through
November&nbsp;1996, he was a Sales and Marketing Manager for
IBM&#146;s Wireless Data Division and a Product Manager at
IBM&#146;s Networking Hardware Division. Mr.&nbsp;Fox has a
M.B.A. from Duke University&#146;s Fuqua School of Business in
Durham, North Carolina and an undergraduate degree in computer
science and electrical engineering from Duke University&#146;s
School of Engineering.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>Richard F. Seifert </B>has been a member of our Board of
Directors since February&nbsp;1999 and has been our Co-Chief
Executive Officer since February&nbsp;2001. He was our Vice
President of Operations from March through November&nbsp;1999.
From 1995 through February&nbsp;1999, Mr.&nbsp;Seifert was a
self-employed marketing consultant. Mr.&nbsp;Seifert has a
degree in business administration from Montgomery County College
and Penn State University.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B>Herman Rush </B>has been a member of our Board of Directors
since March&nbsp;2000. Since 1999, Mr.&nbsp;Rush has been
Chairman of the Board and Chief Executive Officer of
Infotainment International, Inc. and related companies that
develop and produce content for the Internet. Since 1998,
Mr.&nbsp;Rush is a partner in Rush Cooperman Associates, LLC, an
Internet development and production company. In
November&nbsp;2000, he became the CEO of Internet Program
Providers, Inc., an Internet distribution/syndication company.
Mr.&nbsp;Rush served as Executive Producer of The Montel
Williams television programs from 1990 through 1997 and
currently is a consultant to the program. Mr.&nbsp;Rush is a
former President and CEO of the Columbia Pictures Television
Group (1980-1988) and a former CEO of Coca-Cola
Telecommunications, Inc. (1988-89).

of New York at Stony Brook in 1993. She received her M.S. degree
(1985)&nbsp;and B.S. degree (1982), both in computer science,

in the Computer Science Department of Fudan University. She has
published 30 papers in international journals and conferences
and has given many talks at international conferences. She is
also the owner of five U.S. patents. Dr.&nbsp;Zhou is currently
the co-chair for the PSIE/ IS&#38;T Document Recognition

several international conferences and journals, including the
SPIE Document Recognition Conference, the Fifth International
Conference on Document Analysis and Information Retrieval, IEEE
Transaction on Pattern Recognition and Machine Intelligence,
Journal of Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing, and
Journal of Electronic Imaging. Dr.&nbsp;Zhou&#146;s research

information retrieval, character recognition, and document
processing.

<P align="left">
<B>Family Relationships</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
There are no family relationships between or among any of our
directors and executive officers.

<P align="left">
<B>Committees of the Board of Directors</B>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Our Board of Directors is responsible for establishing broad
corporate policies and for our overall performance. On
February&nbsp;27, 2001 our Board of Directors constituted the
following committees:

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B><I>Employment and Compensation Committee.</I></B><I> </I>The
Employment and Compensation Committee reviews and approves the
Company&#146;s compensation plans covering executive officers
and other key management employees, reviews the competitiveness
of the Company&#146;s total compensation practices, determines
the annual base salaries and incentive awards to be paid to
executive officers, and reviews and approves special hiring and
severance arrangements with executive officers. The Employment
and Compensation Committee currently consists of two members,
Messrs.&nbsp;Rush and Jawerth.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
<B><I>Audit Committee.</I></B><I> </I>The Audit Committee
recommends to the Board for appointment the independent auditors
to be selected to audit the financial statements of the Company.
The Audit Committee discusses with the auditors their
independence and obtains at least annually the auditors&#146;
written statement describing their independent status. The Audit
Committee reviews with management and the independent auditors
the Company&#146;s financial statements and any financial
reports submitted to the public. The Audit Committee also has
periodic discussions with management and the independent
auditors regarding the quality and adequacy of the
Company&#146;s internal controls. The Audit Committee currently
consists of Mr.&nbsp;Rush.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<!-- link2 "Item 6. Executive Compensation." -->

<P align="left">
<B>Employment Agreements</B>

<P align="left">
<B>&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Employment Agreement with Dr.&nbsp;Bjorn
Jawerth</I></B>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Upon the closing of the HSNS&nbsp;&#151; Summus, Ltd. business
combination, the Company entered into a three-year employment
agreement with Dr.&nbsp;Bjorn Jawerth. The employment agreement
provides that Dr. Jawerth will serve as the Company&#146;s
co-Chief Executive Officer (on a temporary basis until a new
chief executive officer is hired) and Chief Scientist.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
The terms of Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth&#146;s employment agreement
provided him with the right to request that he be elected the
Chairman of the Board of the Company&#146;s Board of Directors
upon the Company&#146;s hiring of a new chief executive officer.
Effective immediately following the resignations of Stuart
Diamond (who served as Chairman of the Board) and Wendi Tush as
members of the Company&#146;s Board, the remaining members of
the Board appointed Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth to serve as the Chairman.
Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth is expected to continue to serve in that
capacity through the date of the Company&#146;s annual meeting
of shareholders, which is to be held as soon as reasonably
practicable, at which time all of the Company&#146;s director
nominees will be subject to election by the Company&#146;s
shareholders. Given Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth&#146;s substantial equity
interest in the Company, his re-election as a director is
virtually assured.

<DIV align="left"><FONT size="1">

</FONT></DIV>

<P align="left">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;
Under the employment agreement, Dr.&nbsp;Jawerth is to receive:
<P>
